newsitem.title: TANZANIA: World Bank seeks proof of Tanzania bank restructure.
newsitem.headline: World Bank seeks proof of Tanzania bank restructure.

text.p: The World Bank said on Thursday it wanted proof that the Tanzanian government would restructure and privatise the country's biggest state-owned commercial bank before it would disburse $125 million in loans.

The World Bank's representative in Tanzania, Ron Brigish, told Reuters that only further clarification of the government's plans would enable the Bank to release up to $125 million in Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC).
President Benjamin Mkapa announced on Wednesday that his government would split the National Bank of Commerce (NBC) into two before privatising it later this year or early in 1998.
Brigish said he needed proof that the government was launching the restructuring process before the loan could be released.

"The decision (to split NBC) is not what was expected for the release of funds. What was expected was legal amendments to give effect to the decision and action to actually split the assets of the NBC," Brigish told Reuters.
The NBC was established in 1967 when Tanzania had a socialist system, and operated as a monopoly until 1992 when foreign commercial banks were licensed as part of western-backed economic reforms.
Donors led by the World Bank have demanded sweeping reforms in the bank to allow it operate efficiently and the Bank has withheld the SAC loans to force Mkapa to take action.
The first SAC tranche is $50 million for balance of payments support, payable at the World Bank's discretion. In total up to $25 million is earmarked for NBC restructuring.
Under Mkapa's new plan, the NBC's regional and trade divisions would be combined and operated as a single entity while a micro-finance division would be run separately.

"The World Bank commends the government for its decision to break up and privatise NBC. Privatisation when effectively implemented ... has been needed for some time," Brigish said of the ailing former monopoly.
He urged the government to act quickly and offer the bank for sale "on terms and conditions which prospective purchasers are likely to find attractive."
He said that as in other privatisation deals under way, the success of the NBC sale depended on the contents of the offer.

"The devil is in the details. We (World Bank) look forward to working with the government on these details, and in making NBC's successor institutions profitable and sustainable contributors to Tanzania's development efforts," he added.
Privatisation of the NBC has provoked widespread controversy since the intervention of former president Julius Nyerere.
Nyerere, Tanzania's founding father and a staunch advocate of socialist-style central planning, said the NBC break-up could damage the provision of credit facilities to the rural poor.
Nyerere's detractors replied that the ailing bank was too cash-strapped to offer any credit, and its services were a national embarassment to banking.
In Febuary Mkapa vowed to privatise the bank, saying it was a drain on the public purse, racking up losses of 23.36 billion Tanzanian shillings ($37.5 million) between 1993 and 1996.

Speaking from the central town of Dodoma, presidential spokesman Patrick Chokala told Reuters the National Executive Committee of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party had endorsed Mkapa's decision to split the NBC.

"The next step is just machinery -- it's got to go to parliament for changes to the NBC Act and then the operational process will start," he said. No deadline was given for parliamentary approval. ($ = 623.7 Tanzanian Shillings)
